## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mittavindakajātaka* (Ja 82) is a short birth story preserved in the Ekanipāta of the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional introductory narrative, the Buddha recounted this story while dwelling at Jetavana regarding a self-willed or unruly monk [SuttaCentral]. The incidents of this past birth, set in the dispensation of the past Buddha Kassapa, are not detailed in full here; the text notes that the complete narrative will be related in the Tenth Book (*Dasakanipāta*) within the *Mahāmittavindakajātaka* [SuttaCentral].
Mittavindaka is the central protagonist of a recurrent narrative cycle in Buddhist literature depicting sea voyage, karmic encounters with spirits in ocean mansions, and eventual descent into hell, where he suffers the torment of a razor-sharp wheel revolving on his head due to covetousness and ill-treatment of his mother [Winternitz 1933]. This narrative shares close affinities with northern Sanskrit Buddhist traditions, notably the *Maitrakanyaka-avadāna* (as in *Divyāvadāna* 36) and the legend of Maitrāyajña in the *Mahākarmavibhaṅga*, though in the Sanskrit versions the character undergoing the punishment of the wheel is identified as the Bodhisattva displaying compassionate endurance [Winternitz 1933; Nariman 1919; Kudo 2004].
SuttaCentral lists no direct curated parallels for Ja 82, and DharmaNexus reports no Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language alignments with a match score of 10 or greater [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the text in four modern languages [SuttaCentral].
